title: Start, stop, faster, slower: how a push changes moving things

summary.text: Tap a rolling ball from behind, and it goes faster. Tap it from the front, and it slows down or stops. A push or a pull is called a force. Your child taps, flicks and watches, and finds that the side of the push decides what happens.
summary.art: A girl kneeling on a tiled floor, tapping a rolling ball gently with a rolled-up newspaper, while a grown-up rolls the ball towards her.

intro.hook: Roll a ball slowly across the floor. Can you make it stop without grabbing it?
intro.text: A rolling ball keeps going until something pushes against it. A push from behind makes it faster. A push from the front slows it or stops it. You also find out why a rolling ball stops on its own.
intro.art: A ball rolling across a tiled floor towards a small child's open hand held flat in front of it.

outcomes: By the end I can say that a push or a pull can start a thing moving, and can stop it.
By the end I can make a rolling ball go faster by pushing it the same way it is rolling.
By the end I can make a rolling ball go slower, or stop, by pushing against the way it is rolling.
By the end I can show that a bigger push makes a bigger change.
By the end I can say why a rolling ball slows down and stops on the floor.
By the end I can make a guess, test it, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: A force is a push or a pull. Forces make things start, stop, go faster or go slower.
terms.example: Your foot kicking a ball is a force. So is your hand pulling a door.
terms.art: A child kicking a ball, and another child pulling open a door, each with a small arrow.

terms.meaning: Speed is how fast a thing moves. A fast thing has a high speed. A slow thing has a low speed.
terms.example: A running cheetah has a high speed. A snail has a low speed.
terms.art: A cheetah running and a snail crawling, side by side on one page.

terms.meaning: To speed up means to go faster. A push the same way a thing is moving makes it speed up.
terms.example: When you push a swing from behind, the swing speeds up.
terms.art: A woman pushing a girl on a swing from behind, with the swing moving forward.

terms.meaning: To slow down means to go slower. A push against the way a thing is moving makes it slow down.
terms.example: When you put your feet down on the floor, your swing slows down.
terms.art: A girl on a swing dragging her feet on the ground, with dust puffing up.

explanations.concept: A push or a pull starts a thing, and a push or a pull stops it
explanations.definition: A still thing starts moving only when a force pushes or pulls it. A moving thing stops only when a force pushes or pulls against it.
explanations.description: A ball lying on the floor stays still until you tap it. Once it is rolling, it needs another push to stop. Your hand in front of the ball pushes against it. Starting and stopping both need a force.
examples: In the Tap Test, a still ball started rolling after one tap.
A goalkeeper stops a ball by pushing against it with her hands.
An auto starts when its engine pushes it, and stops when its brakes push against the turning wheels.
explanations.context: This card is about the Tap Test, where you tapped a still ball and a rolling ball.
explanations.art: A still ball with a hand tapping it, and next to it a rolling ball meeting a flat hand that stops it.

explanations.concept: The side of the push decides: faster or slower
explanations.definition: A push the same way a thing is moving makes it go faster. A push against the way it is moving makes it go slower, or stop.
explanations.description: In the Tap Test, a tap from behind made the rolling ball faster. A tap from the front made it slower, or stopped it. The tap was just as gentle each time. Only the side you tapped from changed.
examples: Tapping the ball from behind made it go faster.
Tapping the ball from the front made it slow down or stop.
A cyclist pedals to speed up and squeezes the brakes to slow down.
explanations.context: This card says what you found in the Tap Test, when you tapped from behind and from the front.
explanations.art: Two pictures: a ball with a tap from behind and a long arrow ahead, and a ball with a tap from the front and a short arrow ahead.

explanations.concept: A bigger push makes a bigger change
explanations.definition: A small push makes a small change in speed. A big push makes a big change.
explanations.description: In the Flick Test, the hard flick sent the bottle cap over more tiles than the gentle flick. A fast ball is harder to stop than a slow ball. You can feel this when you catch one.
examples: A gentle flick sent the bottle cap a short way. A hard flick sent it much further.
A fast ball stings your hand more when you catch it than a slow ball.
A heavy cupboard needs a much bigger push to start moving than an empty box.
explanations.context: This card is about the Flick Test, where you flicked a bottle cap gently and hard.
explanations.art: A tiled floor with a bottle cap near a child's fingers after a small flick, and another bottle cap far away after a big flick.

explanations.concept: Why a rolling ball stops on its own
explanations.definition: A rolling ball slows down because the floor and the air push against it all the time. These pushes are small, so the ball slows down slowly.
explanations.description: Nobody touches a rolling ball, but it still stops. The floor rubs against it, and the air pushes against it. These small pushes go against the way the ball is moving. On a towel the rubbing is bigger, so the ball stops sooner. This rubbing push is called friction.
examples: A ball rolls a long way on smooth tiles, and stops quickly on a towel or a dari.
A ceiling fan keeps turning for a while after you switch it off, then slowly stops.
Out in space, far from air and floors, a moving thing keeps going for a very long time.
explanations.context: This card answers why a ball stops when nobody touches it.
explanations.art: A ball rolling from shiny tiles onto a folded towel, and stopping on the towel.

agreed.text: A still thing starts moving only when a force acts on it.
agreed.evidence: A ball on the floor stays still until something pushes it: a hand, a foot, the wind or a slope.

agreed.text: A push the same way as the movement speeds a thing up, and a push against it slows it down.
agreed.evidence: Tapping a rolling ball from behind makes it faster. Tapping it from the front makes it slower. Brakes on bicycles, autos and trains all push against the movement.

agreed.text: Moving things slow down on Earth because the ground and the air push against them.
agreed.evidence: A ball rolls further on smooth tiles than on a towel. Spacecraft far out in space keep moving for years without engines.

challenging.who: A common idea among children and grown-ups, and taught by the Greek thinker Aristotle long ago
challenging.for: Every ball we roll slows down and stops, even when nobody touches it.
challenging.against: The ball stops sooner on a towel than on smooth tiles, so something outside the ball is slowing it. The floor and the air push against it. Where there is almost no air or floor, in space, moving things keep going.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that things stop on their own.

challenging.claim: Hitting a moving thing always makes it go faster.
challenging.who: A common first guess among young children
challenging.for: A kick or a hit usually sends a ball flying.
challenging.against: In the Tap Test, a tap from the front slowed the ball down or stopped it. A hit makes a thing faster only when it pushes the same way the thing is going.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that any hit makes a thing faster.

challenging.claim: Heavy things are harder to start and harder to stop.
challenging.who: What most people feel when they push a cupboard or catch a big ball
challenging.for: A full trolley needs a big push to start, and a big push to stop. An empty one needs only a small push.
challenging.against: Nobody has found a heavy thing that is easy to start or stop with the same push. This idea holds up in every test.
challenging.context: This card is about how heavy things start and stop.

big_questions.q: When you tapped the rolling ball from the front, it slowed down. Was that the same kind of push as the one that started it?
big_questions.hint: Think about what your hand did each time. What was different, only the side?

big_questions.q: If there was no floor and no air at all, would a rolling ball ever stop?
big_questions.hint: What slowed the ball down in your test? What if those were gone?

big_questions.q: When you stand very still, is anything in you still moving?
big_questions.hint: Put a hand on your chest. Feel your breath and your heartbeat.

big_questions.q: The Earth is moving round the Sun right now, very fast. Why can't we feel it?
big_questions.hint: Do you feel a smooth train moving when your eyes are shut? When do you feel it?

story.title: Ammu Stops the Boat
story.note: Alappuzha is a real town in Kerala, with many canals and backwaters where people travel in small boats. Ammu, Ammamma and Kannan are made up. Ammamma means mother's mother in Malayalam.
text: Ammu was six. She lived beside the backwaters in Alappuzha, in Kerala. Her grandmother, Ammamma, had a small wooden boat.
Every morning, Ammamma rowed across the water to buy fish at the market. Today, Ammu was going with her.
Ammamma pushed the boat away from the steps with her foot. The boat began to glide.
She dipped her long oar into the water and pulled it back. The boat moved forward. Pull, glide. Pull, glide.
'Faster, Ammamma!' said Ammu.
Ammamma pulled the oar harder and quicker. The boat went faster. Coconut palms slid past. A line of ducks hurried out of the way.
'Can I steer?' asked Ammu.
'You can stop us at the market steps,' said Ammamma. 'That is the hardest job on a boat.'
Ammu laughed. 'Stopping is easy. You just stop rowing.'
'Show me,' said Ammamma. She lifted her oar out of the water and rested it across her knees.
The boat kept going. It slowed down a little, very slowly. The market steps came closer and closer.
'Stop, boat!' said Ammu. But the boat did not stop.
Bump! The front of the boat knocked against the stone steps. A basket of onions on the steps wobbled. A fish seller laughed and waved.
'Why didn't it stop?' asked Ammu. 'Nobody was rowing.'
'The boat was moving,' said Ammamma. 'A moving boat keeps going until something pushes against it. The water pushes back only a little. So the boat slows down only a little.'
After the market, they rowed home with a basket of fish. When their own steps came near, Ammamma gave Ammu the oar.
'This time, push the water the other way,' said Ammamma. 'Push the oar forward, towards the front of the boat.'
Ammu dipped the oar in. She pushed it forward. It was hard work. The water pushed back on the oar, and the boat slowed down.
She pushed again. The boat slowed more. One more push, and the boat stopped, right beside the steps. It did not even touch them.
'I did it!' said Ammu.
'You did,' said Ammamma. 'Pull the water back, and we go faster. Push it forward, and we slow down. The same oar, the same arms. Only the way you push is different.'
In the evening, Ammu's little cousin Kannan came to play. He was four. He rolled a coconut along the verandah, and it rolled straight towards the steps.
'Stop it, Ammu!' he shouted.
Ammu did not grab it. She put her flat hand gently in front of the coconut. It pushed against her hand and stopped.
'How did you do that?' asked Kannan.
'A push from behind makes it go,' said Ammu. 'A push from the front makes it stop. Ammamma taught me on the boat.'
Kannan put his hand out too, and Ammu rolled the coconut to him, very slowly.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Ammu thinks a boat stops by itself when nobody rows. It does not: it drifts on and bumps the steps. Then she finds that the same oar can speed the boat up or slow it down, depending on which way she pushes the water. Stopping needs a push, just like starting.
ask: Why did the boat bump into the market steps?
What did Ammu do with the oar to stop the boat at home?
How did Ammu stop the rolling coconut without grabbing it?
art: A grandmother in a white mundu rowing a small wooden boat on a green Kerala backwater lined with coconut palms, a girl sitting at the front.
The front of the boat bumping gently into stone market steps, a basket of onions wobbling and a fish seller laughing.
The girl pushing the oar forward in the water and the boat stopping beside the steps.
The girl holding her flat hand in front of a rolling coconut on a verandah, while a small boy watches.

experiments.title: The Tap Test: can one tap make a ball faster, slower or stop?
experiments.context: This is the main experiment of the unit. A grown-up rolls a ball slowly across the floor. You tap it with a rolled-up newspaper: when it is still, from behind, and from the front. What does the same gentle tap do each time?
experiments.question: What happens when you tap a rolling ball from behind? What happens when you tap it from the front?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If you tap a rolling ball from behind, will it go faster, slower, or stop? If you tap it from the front, what will it do? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same ball, the same rolled newspaper and the same gentle tap every time. The grown-up rolls the ball just as slowly each time. Only the side we tap from changes. We try each side 3 times, because one try might be luck.

materials.item: a ball that rolls well, such as a plastic ball, a tennis ball or a rubber ball
a sheet of newspaper, rolled up tight and held with tape or a rubber band
a clear stretch of smooth floor, about 3 big steps long, such as a corridor or a room with the mats moved
3 paper slips: FASTER, SLOWER and STOPPED, or 3 drawings: a cheetah, a snail and a stop hand

schedule.what: Guess, tap a still ball, tap a rolling ball from behind and from the front, then try to stop it with just one tap.

experiments.record: Draw the ball and the newspaper for each tap. Draw a cheetah next to the faster tap and a snail next to the slower tap.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: It started rolling, 3 times out of 3
One just-right tap from the front
Stopped dead on the third try

setup.art: A long tiled corridor. A woman sits at one end with a ball, and a girl kneels halfway along, holding a rolled-up newspaper.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up rolls the ball slowly. You kneel beside its path.

setup.art: A girl walking beside a rolling ball and tapping it gently from behind with a rolled newspaper, the ball shooting ahead.
setup.caption: 2. Tap the rolling ball from behind. What happens?

setup.art: A ball rolling towards a girl who kneels in front of it and taps it gently from the front with a rolled newspaper, the ball slowing.
setup.caption: 3. Now tap it from the front. What happens?

flow.do: 1. Clear a stretch of floor. 2. Roll the newspaper tight. 3. Show your child a gentle tap on your own palm.
flow.say: This is our tapper. Every tap is gentle, like this, tap. We will see what one gentle tap does to a ball.
flow.kid: This is your tapper. Tap gently, like this. Watch what one tap does.
flow.parent: A gentle tap with a rolled newspaper is easier to keep the same than a hand. A tiled floor works best. Move mats and dari out of the way.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the ball. 2. Ask both guesses and the reasons. 3. Your child draws the guesses, and a grown-up writes them in the table.
flow.say: If you tap a rolling ball from behind, what will it do? If you tap it from the front, what will it do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. A tap from behind: faster, slower or stop? A tap from the front? Why?

good: From behind it will go faster, because I am pushing it along.
From the front it will go faster too, because a hit makes things go.
From the front it will stop, because I am in its way.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Do not say what will happen. Many children guess that any tap makes the ball faster. The test will show them.

flow.do: 1. Put the ball still on the floor. 2. Your child taps it once, gently.
flow.say: The ball is still. Give it one gentle tap. What happens?
flow.kid: The ball is still. Tap it once. What happens?

good: It started rolling.
It moved away from the tapper.

flow.parent: This is the first change: starting. A still thing starts moving only when something pushes it.

flow.do: 1. Roll the ball slowly along the floor. 2. Your child walks beside it and taps it gently from behind. 3. Do this 3 times.
flow.say: I will roll the ball slowly. Walk beside it and tap it from behind, gently. Did it speed up, slow down or stop?
flow.kid: Walk beside the ball. Tap it from behind. Faster, slower or stopped?

good: It went faster.
It shot away from me.

flow.parent: Roll the ball really slowly, so your child can walk beside it. If the tap misses, just try again. Put the FASTER slip by the ball each time it speeds up.

flow.do: 1. Your child kneels in the ball's path. 2. Roll the ball slowly towards them. 3. They tap it gently from the front. 4. Do this 3 times.
flow.say: Now kneel in front. I will roll the ball to you. Tap it from the front, just as gently. What happens this time?
flow.kid: Kneel in front. The ball comes to you. Tap it from the front. What happens?

good: It slowed down.
It stopped.
It rolled back the other way.

flow.parent: The ball may slow down, stop, or bounce back, depending on the tap. All three are a push against the way it was rolling. If it bounced back, the tap was a little too big. Put the SLOWER or STOPPED slip by the ball to match what it did.

flow.do: Roll the ball towards your child again. They try to make it stop dead with one tap. Give them 3 or 4 tries.
flow.say: Can you stop the ball dead, with just one tap? Not too hard, not too soft.
flow.kid: Try to stop the ball with one tap. Not too hard. Not too soft.
flow.parent: Too soft, and the ball only slows. Too hard, and it rolls back. A just-right tap stops it. This shows that the size of a push matters too.

flow.do: Ask what was the same and what was different. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Was the tap the same each time? What was different? What did a tap from behind do? And from the front?
flow.kid: Was your tap the same each time? What changed? What did each tap do?

good: Only where I tapped from.
From behind it went faster. From the front it went slower or stopped.

check.q: A ball is rolling. You tap it gently from the front. What happens?
check.why: A push against the way a thing is moving slows it down. A just-right push stops it. A push from behind, the same way it is moving, makes it faster.

flow.parent: Wait for your child's own claim first. Then say it plainly: a push the same way makes it faster, a push against makes it slower.

experiments.title: The Flick Test: does a bigger flick send a bottle cap further?
experiments.context: In this experiment you flick a bottle cap across a tiled floor, first gently and then harder. You count how many tiles it goes over before it stops.
experiments.question: Does a harder flick make a bottle cap go faster and further?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will a hard flick send the cap further than a gentle flick? How many tiles do you think each one will go? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same cap, the same finger and the same starting line every time. Only how hard we flick changes. We flick 3 times for each, because one flick might be luck.

materials.item: a plastic bottle cap, or a flat button
a tiled floor, or a long table with a line every hand-span drawn on paper (if your tiles are very big, use tape marks on the floor one hand-span apart)
a small piece of tape or a chalk line for the start

schedule.what: Guess, flick gently 3 times, flick hard 3 times, and count the tiles each time.

experiments.record: Draw a row of tiles. Put a small dot where the gentle flicks stopped and a big dot where the hard flicks stopped.

setup.art: A plastic bottle cap at a strip of tape on a tiled floor, and a child's finger curled ready to flick it.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cap on the start line.

setup.art: A bottle cap sliding across floor tiles after a flick, with a girl counting the tiles with her finger.
setup.caption: 2. Flick it. Count the tiles it went over.

flow.do: 1. Put tape on the floor as a start line. 2. Show a gentle flick and a hard flick. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: We will flick the cap gently, then hard. Which one will go further? How many tiles? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Gentle flick or hard flick: which goes further? Why?

good: The hard flick, because it is a bigger push.
They will go the same.

flow.do: 1. Your child flicks the cap gently 3 times from the line. 2. Count the tiles each time, together. 3. A grown-up writes the numbers.
flow.say: Flick it gently. Watch it go. Now count the tiles it went over. Let's do it 3 times.
flow.kid: Flick gently. Count the tiles. Do it 3 times.
flow.parent: Count a tile if the cap went past its middle. If your tiles are very big, stick small bits of tape on the floor, one hand-span apart, and count those. On a table, use hand-spans drawn on paper.

flow.do: 1. Your child flicks hard 3 times. 2. Count the tiles. 3. A grown-up writes the numbers.
flow.say: Now flick it hard. Was it faster? Count the tiles.
flow.kid: Now flick hard. Was it faster? Count the tiles.

good: The hard flick went faster.
It went over more tiles.

flow.parent: Keep the room clear so the cap does not slide under furniture. A hard flick is still a finger flick, not a throw. Flicks are never exactly the same, so one hard flick may go less far than one gentle flick. That is why we flick 3 times.

flow.do: Ask why the cap stopped at all, then the check question.
flow.say: Nobody stopped the cap. Why did it stop? What was pushing against it?
flow.kid: Nobody stopped the cap. Why did it stop?

good: The floor rubbed it.
The floor pushed against it until it stopped.

check.q: Which flick sent the cap further?
check.why: A bigger push makes a bigger change. The hard flick gave the cap more speed, so it went further before the floor slowed it down.

activities.title: The Ceiling Fan Watch: start, faster, slower, stop
activities.context: In this activity you watch a ceiling fan start, speed up, slow down and stop. You find out that the fan keeps turning for a while after it is switched off.

materials.item: a ceiling fan with a switch and a speed knob

activities.safety: A grown-up works the switch. Stay well away from the fan blades and never throw things at a fan.

schedule.what: Watch the fan start, speed up, slow down and stop, and count how long it keeps turning after switching off.

activities.record: Draw the fan four times: still, slow, fast, and slowing down. Draw lines round the fast one to show it is fast.

setup.art: A grown-up pointing to a ceiling fan switch on the wall while a boy sits on a mat across the room, looking up at the still fan.
setup.caption: 1. Sit on a mat to one side and look up at the still fan.

setup.art: A ceiling fan with blurred blades, and the boy on the mat to one side counting on his fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Switch it on, then off. Count until it stops.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits on a mat to one side of the fan, not right under it. 2. Switch the fan on at the lowest speed.
flow.say: Watch the fan. It is still. Now I switch it on. Does it go fast straight away?
flow.kid: Watch the fan. Does it go fast straight away?

good: It started slowly.
It got faster and faster.

flow.parent: The motor pushes the blades round. It takes a few seconds to bring them up to speed.

flow.do: Turn the speed knob up, then down.
flow.say: Now I turn the knob up. What happens? Now down. What happens?
flow.kid: The knob goes up. What happens? Now down?

good: It went faster.
Then it went slower.

flow.do: 1. Switch the fan off. 2. Count together, one, two, three, until the blades stop.
flow.say: Now I switch it off. Is it still turning? Let's count until it stops.
flow.kid: The fan is off. Is it still turning? Count until it stops.

good: It was already moving.
Nothing stopped it straight away.

flow.parent: Most fans keep turning for a good while, often half a minute or more. The air and the rubbing inside the fan slowly stop it.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: The fan was off, but it kept turning. What slowed it down in the end?
flow.kid: What slowed the fan down in the end?

check.q: A fan keeps turning after you switch it off, and then it stops. Why does it stop?
options: The air and the rubbing inside slowly push against it
Nothing pushes it. It just stops
check.why: A moving thing keeps moving until something pushes against it. The air and the rubbing inside the fan are small pushes, so the fan slows down slowly.

activities.title: Window Watch: who starts and who stops?
activities.context: In this activity you look out of a window or a balcony for 5 minutes. You spot things that start, stop, speed up and slow down: autos, scooters, people, crows and pigeons.

materials.item: a window or a balcony with a view of a road, a path or the sky
a sheet of paper with 4 boxes drawn on it, each with a word: START, STOP, FASTER, SLOWER (or a drawing: a green light, a red light, a cheetah, a snail)

schedule.what: Watch for 5 minutes, put a tick in a box for each change you see, then talk about what pushed each one.

activities.record: Your paper with ticks in the four boxes, and a drawing of one thing you saw stop.

setup.art: A girl and a grown-up at a flat window, looking down at a road with autos, a scooter and a bus stopping at a stop.
setup.caption: 1. Look out for 5 minutes.

setup.art: A paper with four boxes, START, STOP, FASTER and SLOWER, with ticks in each, and a crayon beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Tick a box for each change you see.

flow.do: Watch out of the window together. Each time your child sees something start, stop, speed up or slow down, they put a tick in that box.
flow.say: Look! That auto is slowing down. Tick SLOWER. Can you spot something that starts?
flow.kid: Look out. Tick a box when something starts, stops, goes faster or slower.
flow.parent: Buses at a stop, autos at a signal, a person walking then running, a crow landing on a wall: all good. If the road is quiet, watch birds, or people in the corridor.

flow.do: Pick two things your child saw, and ask what pushed them.
flow.say: The crow landed on the wall. What did she do to slow down? The bus stopped. What pushed against it?
flow.kid: How did the crow slow down? What stopped the bus?

ask.q: What did the crow do to slow down?
good: She spread her wings and tail wide.
She flapped against the way she was going.

flow.parent: A landing bird spreads her wings and tail and tips them against the air, pushing the air forward to slow down. A bus slows when its brakes press on the wheels.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Here is a question about the auto we saw.
flow.kid: Here is a question.

check.q: An auto slows down at a red light. What made it slow down?
options: Its brakes pushed against the turning wheels
The red light pulled it back
It ran out of speed by itself
check.why: A moving thing slows down when something pushes against its movement. The brakes press on the wheels and slow them down.

activities.safety: At a balcony, stay behind the grill or railing and never lean over it.

activities.title: Soft Stop, Hard Stop: catch the rolling ball
activities.context: In this activity you roll a ball into different things: a pillow, a big book standing up, and a paper tent. Which one stops the ball? Which one only slows it down?

materials.item: a pillow or a folded blanket, propped upright against a wall or the sofa
a big book, standing open like a wall
a sheet of paper folded into a tent

schedule.what: Roll the ball into each thing in turn and see whether it stops, slows or bounces back.

activities.record: Draw the three stoppers. Next to each, draw what the ball did: a stop hand, a snail, or a curved arrow going back.

setup.art: A pillow, a book standing open and a paper tent in a row on a tiled floor, with a ball ready to roll at them.
setup.caption: 1. Set up three stoppers.

setup.art: A ball knocking over a small paper tent and rolling on more slowly, while a boy watches.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the ball into each one. What does it do?

flow.do: Set up the three stoppers a few steps from your child. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: Which of these will stop the ball? Which one will only slow it down? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which one will stop the ball? Which will only slow it? Why?

good: The book will stop it, because it is heavy.
The paper will fall over, because it is light.

flow.do: Your child rolls the ball into each stopper, at the same gentle speed, twice each.
flow.say: Roll it into the paper tent. What happened? Now the pillow. Now the book.
flow.kid: Roll the ball into each one. What happens?

good: The paper fell over and the ball kept going, slower.
The pillow stopped it softly.
The book stopped it, and it bounced back a bit.

flow.parent: The paper tent pushes back only a little, so the ball only slows. The pillow squashes and stops it gently. The hard book pushes back quickly, so the ball may bounce.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: The paper tent fell over. Why did the ball keep going?
flow.kid: Why did the ball keep going past the paper?

check.q: The ball knocked over the paper tent and kept rolling, but slower. Why?
options: The paper pushed back only a little
check.why: To stop a moving ball, something must push against it hard enough. The paper pushed back a little, so the ball only slowed down.

games.title: Which Way to Push?
games.players: 1 to 4 players and a grown-up who reads the cards. With two people, the grown-up reads and the child plays.
games.context: This is a card game. Each card shows something moving and what you want it to do. You put a paper arrow down to show which way to push: the same way it is moving, or against it.

items.f: A swing is moving forward. Make it go FASTER.
items.b: Push the same way: from behind, as it swings away.

items.f: A ball is rolling to the door. Make it STOP.
items.b: Push against it: put a hand in front.

items.f: A toy car is rolling slowly. Make it go FASTER.
items.b: Push the same way: tap it from behind.

items.f: A bicycle is going down a hill. Make it go SLOWER.
items.b: Push against it: squeeze the brakes.

items.f: A boat is gliding to the steps. Make it STOP.
items.b: Push against it: push the oar forward in the water.

items.f: A ball is lying still. Make it START.
items.b: Push it any way you like: a tap starts it rolling.

items.f: A duck is flying down to the pond. She wants to SLOW DOWN.
items.b: Push against the way she is going: feet out in front, wings spread wide.

items.f: A friend on roller skates is rolling slowly. Make her go FASTER.
items.b: Push the same way: a gentle push on her back.

rules: Cut out the 8 cards and the 2 arrows: green is SAME WAY and red is AGAINST.
Put the cards in a pile, front side up. The grown-up reads the front of the top card to the player whose turn it is.
The player says SAME WAY or AGAINST, and lays the green or red arrow next to the card.
The grown-up reads the back. A right answer wins the card. For a START card, any arrow is right, because a still thing has no way yet.
A wrong answer: the grown-up shows it with a ball or a hand, and the card goes to the bottom of the pile to come round again.
Players take turns. The game ends when all 8 cards are won. Whoever has the most cards wins, and a tie means you all win. With two people, the child plays and tries to win all 8.

setup.art: A woman reading a card while a girl holds a green paper arrow and a red paper arrow.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up reads a card.

setup.art: A card that reads "A swing is moving forward. Make it go FASTER.", and a green paper arrow laid next to it.
setup.caption: 2. Lay down the arrow: same way or against.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and the two arrows. 2. Explain green means SAME WAY and red means AGAINST.
flow.say: Green means push the same way it is moving. Red means push against it. Listen to each card and pick an arrow.
flow.kid: Green: push the same way. Red: push against it. Pick one for each card.

flow.do: Read the cards one by one. Your child picks an arrow and says why.
flow.say: A ball is rolling to the door. You want it to stop. Which arrow? Why?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick an arrow. Say why.

good: To stop it you push against it.
Like my tap from the front.

flow.parent: Link each card to the Tap Test. If your child picks the wrong arrow, act it out with a ball.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Last one, about the swing.
flow.kid: Last one.

check.q: A swing is moving away from you. You want it to go higher and faster. How do you push?
options: The same way it is moving, from behind
check.why: A push the same way a thing is moving speeds it up. That is why we push a swing from behind as it moves away.

games.title: Cheetah, Snail, Statue
games.players: 2 or more players. One is the caller, a grown-up first.
games.context: This is a moving game. The caller holds up a card, and the players walk faster, slower, start or stop. Then you say what your feet did.

items.b: Start walking. Your feet push back on the floor.
Walk faster. Push harder with your feet.
Walk slower. Push less with your feet.
Stop and freeze. Your feet push forward on the floor to stop you.

rules: Clear a space. Players walk, never run, on a floor that is not slippery.
The caller holds up GO, CHEETAH, SNAIL or STATUE, in any order. Players follow the card.
After each STATUE, the caller asks one player what their feet did to stop.
After 4 STATUEs, the caller swaps with another player. The game ends when every player has been the caller once.
games.safety: Walk, do not run. Play barefoot or in shoes, not in socks on tiles, so nobody slips.

setup.art: A girl holding up a snail card, and two children walking slowly in a cleared room.
setup.caption: 1. The caller holds up a card.

setup.art: Two children frozen like statues mid-step, one leaning back slightly, with feet planted.
setup.caption: 2. On STATUE, freeze. What did your feet do?

flow.do: Clear a space and read the rules.
flow.say: I will hold up a card. Do what it says. Walk, never run.
flow.kid: Watch the card. Do what it says. Walk, don't run.

flow.do: Hold up the cards in any order, about every 10 seconds. After each STATUE, ask what their feet did. After 4 STATUEs, swap callers.
flow.say: Statue! Freeze! What did your feet do to stop you?
flow.kid: Freeze! What did your feet do to stop you?

ask.q: What did your feet do to stop?
good: They pushed forward on the floor.
I pressed my feet down on the floor.

flow.parent: To stop, our feet push forward against the floor, and the floor pushes back on us. That push against our movement is what stops us.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: One last question.
flow.kid: One last question.

check.q: You are walking fast and want to stop. What do your feet do?
options: Push back, like when you start
check.why: To start, your feet push back on the floor. To stop, they push forward. The floor pushes back on you, against your movement, and you stop.

projects.title: My Start and Stop Book
projects.context: In this project you make a small book over 3 days. Each day you find things that start, stop, go faster or go slower, and draw them.

materials.item: 2 sheets of paper, folded in half and tied with thread into a little book

schedule.what: Make the book. Draw two things you saw START and STOP today, and what pushed them.
Draw two things you saw go FASTER and SLOWER, and what pushed them.
Draw yourself starting and stopping. Read the book to someone in the family.

projects.record: The finished book, with a drawing and a push arrow on every page.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper folded and tied with thread into a little book, titled 'Start and Stop'.
setup.caption: 1. Fold and tie the book.

setup.art: An open page with a crayon drawing of a bus stopping at a bus stop, and a red arrow at its front wheels.
setup.caption: 2. Draw what you saw, with an arrow for the push.

flow.do: 1. Make the book. 2. A grown-up writes START and STOP on the first two pages. 3. Your child draws one thing for each.
flow.say: What did you see start today? What did you see stop? Draw them. Draw an arrow for the push.
flow.kid: Draw something that started and something that stopped. Add an arrow for the push.
flow.parent: Good ideas: a mixie starting, a ball stopping, a door being pushed open, a bus stopping.

flow.do: A grown-up writes FASTER and SLOWER on the next pages. Your child draws one thing for each.
flow.say: What did you see go faster today? What went slower? What pushed them?
flow.kid: Draw something going faster and something going slower.

flow.do: Your child draws themself starting and stopping, then reads the book to someone.
flow.say: Draw yourself starting to walk and stopping. Now read your book to someone in the family.
flow.kid: Draw yourself starting and stopping. Read your book to someone.

check.q: Which of these needs a push or a pull?
options: Starting, stopping, going faster and going slower
check.why: Every change in how a thing moves needs a force: starting, stopping, speeding up and slowing down.

challenges.title: Stop the Ball on the Line
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A ball rolls down a slope. You must make it stop on a line drawn on the floor, without touching it.
challenges.problem: A ball rolls down a slope made of a tray leaning on two books. Can you make the ball stop on a line, about one big step from the bottom, without anyone touching it?
constraints: Nobody may touch the ball once it starts.
The ball must stop on the line, not before and not after.
materials: a tray or a big book leaning on two books, as a slope
a towel, a dupatta or a dari
a strip of tape or chalk for the line
general: Long jumpers land in a pit of soft sand, which stops them gently.
Some steep mountain roads in the world have runaway truck ramps filled with loose gravel or sand, to slow down trucks whose brakes have failed.
Cricket nets and goal nets stretch and slowly stop the ball.
creative: Lay a towel on the floor after the slope. The rubbing slows the ball, so it stops sooner.
Fold the towel to make it thicker, or lay it out only partly, until the ball stops right on the line.
Stand a pillow right at the line as a soft wall, so the ball stops gently at the line.
challenges.your_turn: Try two ways of stopping the ball on the line. Which works better? Why do you think so?

setup.art: A tray leaning on two books as a slope, a ball at the top, and a tape line on the floor one big step from the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Make a slope and a line.

setup.art: A towel laid across the floor before the tape line, and a ball stopped right on the line.
setup.caption: 2. Use home things to stop the ball on the line.

flow.do: Read the problem. Let the ball roll once with nothing in its way.
flow.say: Watch where the ball stops with nothing in its way. It probably goes past the line. If it stops short, move the line further away. How could we make it stop sooner?
flow.kid: Watch the ball. Does it stop before the line or go past it? How can you make it stop on the line?

good: Something rough, like a towel.
Something soft in front, like a pillow.

flow.do: Your child tries their ideas. Let them change one thing at a time.
flow.say: Try your idea. Did it stop before the line, on it, or after it? What will you change?
flow.kid: Try your idea. Before the line, on it or after it? Change one thing.
flow.parent: Let your child try and fail. The towel slows the ball by rubbing. Moving the towel nearer or further changes where it stops.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Why did the ball stop sooner on the towel?
flow.kid: Why did the towel help?

check.q: The ball stopped sooner on a towel than on the bare floor. Why?
options: The towel rubbed against the ball more, pushing against its movement
The towel pulled the ball forward
The ball was too heavy to roll
check.why: The rubbing between the towel and the ball pushes against the ball's movement. The bigger rubbing on a towel slows it down sooner. This rubbing is called friction.

items.p: Draw a line from each wish to the push that does it.
pairs: Make a rolling ball go faster
items.why: Starting, speeding up and stopping all need a push. A push from behind speeds a ball up, and a push from the front stops it.
items.art: Three balls on the left, still, rolling and rolling, and three hands on the right, tapping, pushing from behind and held in front.

items.p: Draw the Tap Test: the ball, the rolled newspaper, and you tapping it from the front.
items.a: A ball, a newspaper tapper in front of it, and the child kneeling.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the tapper on the side of the ball that faces where it is going.
items.art: A blank box with a line for the floor.

items.p: Circle in green the ones that are speeding up. Circle in red the ones that are slowing down.
items: A bus leaving the bus stop
A bicycle with the brakes on
A duck landing on the water
items.why: A push the same way as the movement speeds a thing up. A push against the movement slows it down.

items.p: A tap from the front makes a rolling ball go faster.
items.why: False. A tap from the front pushes against the way the ball is moving, so it slows it down or stops it.

items.p: Three of these are speeding up. Which one is slowing down?
opts: A bus stopping at a red light
items.why: The bus stopping is slowing down. Its brakes push against the turning wheels. The others are all speeding up.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: what did your tap do when you tapped the ball from behind?
items.a: It made the ball go faster, because I pushed it the same way it was rolling.
items.why: A strong answer says what the ball did and that the push went the same way as the ball.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 1, flicks a bottle cap gently. It goes 2 tiles. Then she flicks it hard. What will happen?
items.why: A bigger push makes a bigger change. The hard flick makes the cap faster, so it goes further before it stops.

items.p: Put the Tap Test in order.
items: Tap the rolling ball from the front
Tap the rolling ball from behind
a: Tap the rolling ball from behind
Tap the rolling ball from the front
items.why: First we guess. Then we start a still ball, then tap a rolling ball from behind, then from the front.

items.p: Draw something in your home that starts and stops many times a day. Draw an arrow for the push that starts it.
items.a: Any thing that starts and stops, such as a door, a mixie, a fan or a person, with an arrow.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a real thing and an arrow showing a push or a pull on it.

items.p: The ceiling fan was still, then on, then fast, then off. Under each picture, say START, FASTER or SLOWER, and a grown-up writes it.
items.why: Switching on starts the fan. Turning up the knob makes the motor push harder, so it goes faster. Switching off lets the air slow it down.
items.art: Three drawings of a ceiling fan: blades just moving, blades blurred, blades slowing, each with an empty label.

items.p: Lakshmi and her friend Farhan roll a ball across the floor in Hyderabad. It slows down and stops.

views.says: The ball stopped by itself. Nobody touched it.
Something did stop it. The floor rubbed against it. On the towel it stopped even sooner.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence. For Lakshmi: the ball stopped sooner on a towel, so something outside the ball slows it. For Farhan: no person touched it, and the push from the floor is too small to see.
items.why: Both see something true. No hand touched the ball, but the floor and the air push against it all the time. That is why it stops sooner on a rough towel.

items.p: Draw Ammu's boat stopping at the steps. Draw her oar pushing the water forward.
items.a: A boat, a girl, and an oar pushing towards the front of the boat.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the oar pushing towards the front. Pushing the water forward slows the boat down.
items.art: A blank box with wavy lines for water at the bottom.

items.p: A fast ball needs a bigger push to stop it than a slow ball.
items.why: True. A bigger change needs a bigger push. That is why a fast ball stings your hand more when you catch it.

items.p: In Soft Stop, Hard Stop, what did each stopper do to the ball?
items.why: A pillow, a blanket and a book push back hard enough to stop the ball. Paper pushes back only a little, so the ball only slows.

items.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 1, flicked a cap 3 times gently. It went 2 tiles, 1 tile and 2 tiles. How many tiles in all?
items.why: 2 and 1 make 3. 3 and 2 make 5.

items.p: Many people think that things stop by themselves. What test could you do to show that something is slowing them down?
items.a: Roll the same ball on tiles and on a towel. If it stops sooner on the towel, something outside the ball is slowing it.
items.why: A strong answer suggests changing what the ball rolls on and keeping everything else the same.

items.p: Look at the picture of a girl on a swing. Say what each push does: FASTER or SLOWER, and a grown-up writes it.
labels: A grown-up pushes from behind as the swing goes away
The girl drags her feet on the ground
items.why: A push the same way as the swing speeds it up. Feet dragging on the ground push against it, so it slows down.
items.art: A girl on a swing, with a grown-up behind her and her feet just touching the ground, and two empty labels.

items.p: Two trolleys get the same gentle push. One is empty and one is full of heavy bags. Which one speeds up more?
items.why: A heavy thing needs a bigger push to change its speed. The same push changes the empty trolley more.

items.p: In space, a ball that is pushed gently keeps moving for a very long time.
items.why: True. In space there is almost no air and no floor to push against the ball, so nothing slows it down.

items.p: A cricketer pulls her hands back as she catches a fast ball. Why?
opts: The ball slows down over a longer time, so it stings less
items.why: Pulling the hands back makes the ball slow down more slowly. The push on her hands is then smaller.

quiz.p: A ball is lying still on the floor. What will make it start rolling?
quiz.why: A still thing starts moving only when a force pushes or pulls it.

quiz.p: A ball is rolling away from you. You tap it gently from behind. What happens?
quiz.why: A push the same way a thing is moving makes it go faster.

quiz.p: A ball is rolling towards you. You put your flat hand in front of it. What happens?
quiz.why: Your hand pushes against the way the ball is moving, so it stops.
A force is a push or a pull. How fast something goes is its speed.

quiz.p: Which flick sends a bottle cap furthest?
quiz.why: A bigger push makes a bigger change, so a hard flick makes the cap faster and it goes further.

quiz.p: Why does a rolling ball slow down and stop on the floor?
opts: The floor and the air push against it
Nothing pushes it. It just stops
quiz.why: The floor rubs against the ball and the air pushes on it. These small pushes against its movement slow it down.

quiz.p: You open a drawer by its handle, and it slides towards you. What started it moving?
quiz.why: A force is a push or a pull. Pulling the handle makes the drawer start to move.

quiz.p: Divya, a girl in Class 1, wants her swing to go slower. What can she do?
opts: Drag her feet on the ground
Ask for a push from behind
quiz.why: Her feet on the ground push against the swing's movement, so it slows down.

quiz.p: Meera, a girl in Class 1, guesses that a tap from the front will make a ball go faster. She tests it, and the ball slows down. What should she say?
opts: My guess was wrong. A tap from the front slows it down.
She should still say it goes faster.
quiz.why: A good scientist trusts what the test shows, and changes their idea. A wrong guess is how we learn.

quiz.p: Ammu, a girl in a story, wants to stop her boat. Which way should she push her oar?
opts: Forward, towards the front of the boat
She should not use the oar
quiz.why: Pulling the water back makes the boat go faster. Pushing it forward pushes against the boat's movement, so it slows down and stops.

applications: Brakes on bicycles, autos, buses and trains push against the turning wheels to slow them down.
A parachute is a big cloth that the air pushes up against, so a person falls slowly.
At the end of a railway line, a strong buffer stop pushes against a train that rolls too far.
Cricketers pull their hands back as they catch a fast ball, so the ball slows down over a longer time and stings less.
Seat belts hold passengers back when a car stops suddenly, pushing against their forward movement.

open_questions.q: Why does a moving thing keep moving at all?
open_questions.why_open: We know that a moving thing keeps going until a force changes it. But nobody knows for sure why things carry their movement in the first place. Some scientists think it has to do with all the stars and galaxies in the universe. They still argue about it.

open_questions.q: How does a crow know exactly how hard to push against the air to land on a thin wire?
open_questions.why_open: Birds land on wires and branches with great care, sensing their speed and changing their push again and again. Scientists study how they judge it so well, and much is still unknown.

open_questions.q: Is anything in the universe completely still?
open_questions.why_open: The Earth spins and goes round the Sun. The Sun moves round the middle of our galaxy. Even the tiny particles in a still stone jiggle. Nobody has found anything that is perfectly still.

ask_kids: What do you push to start the mixie? What stops it?
How does a bus slow down at a bus stop?
When you run and want to stop, what do your feet do?
Why does a ball roll further on the tiles than on the dari?
Can you make your swing go faster? How?

jokes.j: Why did the ball stop rolling?
What did the brakes say to the bicycle?
What did the ball say to the towel?
What did the cheetah say to the snail?
jokes.a: Race you! And the snail said, I will get there... eventually.

jokes.j: Why did the duck skid to a stop on the pond?
Why did the swing never win an argument?
jokes.a: It kept going back and forth!

jokes.j: Why was the ball so tired of rolling?
jokes.a: Because everybody kept pushing it around!

jokes.j: Why can't a bicycle stand up by itself?

maths.problem: In the Flick Test, Kavya, a girl in Class 1, flicks a cap. Her gentle flick went 2 tiles. Her hard flick went 7 tiles. How many more tiles did the hard flick go?
maths.explain: Count on from 2 to 7: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. That is 5 more. So the bigger push sent the cap 5 tiles further.
maths.context: This is about the Flick Test, where you flicked a bottle cap gently and hard.
maths.why_maths: Taking the small number from the big one shows how much difference the bigger push made.

maths.problem: Farhan, a boy in Class 1, flicks a cap three times: 4 tiles, 1 tile and 6 tiles. One was gentle, one was medium and one was hard. Put them in order from the gentlest to the hardest flick.
maths.explain: A bigger push sends the cap further. So the gentlest flick went the shortest way, 1 tile, and the hardest went the furthest, 6 tiles.
maths.context: This is about the Flick Test, where you flicked a bottle cap and counted tiles.
maths.why_maths: Putting the numbers in order lets us guess which flick was which, without seeing them.

maths.problem: In Window Watch, Nila, a girl in Class 1, made 3 ticks for START, 5 ticks for STOP, 2 ticks for FASTER and 4 ticks for SLOWER. Which change did she see most? Which least?
maths.answer: She saw STOP most, 5 times. She saw FASTER least, 2 times.
maths.explain: 5 is the biggest number, so STOP came most often. 2 is the smallest, so FASTER came least often. On a busy road, things stop a lot at signals and bus stops.
maths.context: This is about Window Watch, where you ticked a box for every change you saw.
maths.why_maths: Counting the ticks shows at a glance what happens most on our road.

warmup.q: What is a push or a pull called?
How do you make a swing go faster?
warmup.a: Push it from behind, the same way it is moving.

warmup.q: How do you stop a rolling ball without grabbing it?
warmup.a: Put a flat hand in front of it, pushing against it.

warmup.q: Does a hard flick or a gentle flick go further?
warmup.a: A hard flick. A bigger push makes a bigger change.

warmup.q: Why does a ball stop sooner on a towel?
warmup.a: The towel rubs against it more, pushing against its movement.

warmup.q: What do a duck's feet do when she lands?
warmup.a: They push forward on the water, to slow her down.

roots.context: We have tapped, flicked and stopped moving things. Now we ask what the Tap Test tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: One gentle tap started the still ball, made the rolling ball faster, and made it slower or stop. The tap was the same each time. Only the side you tapped from changed. So speeding up and slowing down are one kind of change, and the push's direction decides which.
deep_truth.habit: We think of going and stopping as opposites with different causes: a push makes things go, and they stop on their own. The test shows one cause for both. A push the same way speeds a thing up, and a push the other way slows it down.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Tap Test, the same rolled newspaper and the same gentle tap made the ball faster from behind and slower from the front. A just-right tap from the front stopped it dead, and a bigger one sent it back.

three.who_am_i: You start and stop many times a day. Each time, your feet push on the floor, back to start and forward to stop.
three.what_is_life: Every living being that moves pushes on something to start and to stop. A duck pushes the water, and a crow pushes the air.
three.what_is_this_world: Everything in the world is moving somehow. Pushes and pulls change how fast it moves, all the time.

roots.thread: Starting, stopping, speeding up and slowing down look like four different things. Underneath, they are one change with one kind of cause, a push or a pull. A ball, a boat, an auto and a swing all follow it. Everything is conscious, and each moving thing meets every push in its own way.

teachings.teaching: Jain thinkers taught that one thing, called dharma, helps things move, and another, called adharma, helps things come to rest.
teachings.link: These thinkers saw that coming to rest needs a cause, just as moving does. In the Tap Test, stopping the ball needed a push too.

teachings.teaching: Who can make muddy water clear? Let it be still, and slowly it becomes clear. Who can bring stillness to life? Let it move, and slowly it comes alive.
teachings.link: In our tests, a rolling ball slowly became still, and a still ball began to roll with one tap.

science.text: A moving thing keeps the same speed until a force acts on it. A force the same way speeds it up, and a force against it slows it down.
Why moving things carry their movement at all is still argued about. The scientist Ernst Mach suggested it may come from all the matter in the universe.

other_view.view: A ball's movement is fully explained by the forces on it. For them, nothing more is going on in the ball, and feeling belongs only to living beings with nerves.

practice.title: Slow down to still
practice.say: Stand up and walk slowly across the room. Now walk even slower, like a snail. Slower still. Now stop. Feel what your feet did to stop you. Stand very still and close your eyes. Is anything in you still moving? Feel your breath going in and out.
practice.kid: Walk slowly. Walk slower, like a snail. Stop. What did your feet do? Stand still. Shut your eyes. Feel your breath move.

ask: When you start to walk, what pushes you forward: you, or the floor?
When you stand very still, is anything in you still moving?
Who stopped Ammu's boat: Ammu, the oar, or the water?
roots.art: A girl standing very still with her eyes closed in a quiet room, one hand on her chest, a ball resting still on the floor beside her.

how_we_found_out.context: Do moving things stop on their own? This card tells how people slowly found out.
how_we_found_out.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker; Galileo, an Italian scientist; John Philoponus, a thinker in Alexandria, Egypt; Ibn Sina, a Persian thinker and doctor; and later Isaac Newton, with Émilie du Châtelet, a French scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: A thrown stone is pushed along by the air behind it, and a moving thing stops on its own when the push ends.
how_we_found_out.story: Long ago in Greece, the thinker Aristotle asked why a thrown stone keeps flying after it leaves your hand. He said the air behind it pushes it along. Many people believed this for hundreds of years. In the 500s, John Philoponus, in Alexandria in Egypt, said this was wrong. Air slows a stone down, he said, so it cannot be pushing it. He said the thrower's hand gives the stone a push that it carries inside, and that this push slowly wears out. Around 1020, the Persian thinker Ibn Sina went further. He said the push a stone carries would never wear out by itself. In empty space, with no air, a moving thing would keep going and never stop. Around 1600, Galileo in Italy rolled balls down slopes and saw that they slowed less on smoother boards. In 1687, Isaac Newton wrote it as a law: a moving thing keeps going until a force changes it. In France, Émilie du Châtelet translated Newton's book into French and explained it. Her translation, published in 1759, is still read today.

Cambridge Primary Science Stage 1, 5.4 Changing movement: making a ball go faster, slower and stop. The Level 3 unit on this subtopic covers changing shape (squashing, bending, bouncing prints), so this unit uses the Tap Test, the Flick Test, the ceiling fan, Window Watch and Soft Stop, Hard Stop instead.
science: Newton's first and second laws: a force changes speed, and a force against the motion slows it. Any introductory physics text.
John Philoponus (6th century) and Ibn Sina (Book of Healing, Physics) on impressed force and inclination (mayl). See the history of the theory of impetus.
Émilie du Châtelet's French translation of Newton's Principia, published in 1759, after her death in 1749.
Mach's principle, Ernst Mach (1883): the idea that inertia comes from the rest of the matter in the universe. Still debated.
Tattvartha Sutra 5.17 on dharma and adharma as the media of motion and rest.
